title: Transformation of lung adenocarcinoma to small cell lung cancer following osimertinib treatment: a case report and literature review
author: Linwu Kuang; Peng Wang; Lin Zhou; Yangkai Li
text:
Abstract
Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) effectively treat EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma, demonstrating initial efficacy but eventually leading to acquired resistance. Small cell transformation is a rare resistance mechanism to EGFR-TKIs in lung adenocarcinoma, which can complicate clinical diagnosis and treatment. We present a patient with lung adenocarcinoma who underwent a prior pneumonectomy and adjuvant chemotherapy and was treated with osimertinib after the recurrence of lung cancer. Small cell transformation occurred approximately 20 months after starting osimertinib treatment. After this transformation, the patient underwent lung radiotherapy and cisplatin–etoposide chemotherapy, which stabilized the disease. Following the confirmation of small cell lung cancer (SCLC) via thyroid puncture, treatments with irinotecan, irinotecan plus atezolizumab, thyroid radiotherapy, adrenal radiotherapy, and head radiotherapy were sequentially administered, yet the disease continued to progress. The patient succumbed to the disease in May 2023 because of progression and organ failure, with an overall survival of 52.7 months, including 16 months post small cell transformation. This case highlights the possibility of osimertinib causing lung adenocarcinoma to transform into SCLC and underscores rebiopsies’ importance in identifying resistance mechanisms to EGFR-TKIs. Increased levels of neuron-specific enolase and pro-gastrin releasing peptide can signal early transformation into SCLC.
Keywords: case report, epidermal growth factor receptor-tyrosine kinase inhibitors, lung adenocarcinoma, small cell lung cancer transformation, small cell lung cancer
Introduction
Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) are the recommended first-line therapy for lung adenocarcinoma harboring EGFR mutations, demonstrating substantial improvements in patient survival outcomes. Typically, patients experience disease progression after 12 months of TKI treatment [1]. The predominant resistance mechanism to EGFR-TKIs is currently the T790M mutation, representing 50–60% of all cases. Other mechanisms include HER2 amplification, AXL receptor tyrosine kinase activation, mesenchymal-epithelial transition amplification, and small cell lung cancer (SCLC) transformation. Although SCLC transformation accounts for only 5–10% of cases [2], it significantly complicates diagnosis and treatment. Research on the histological transformation of lung adenocarcinoma to SCLC remains limited, with the underlying mechanisms yet to be fully elucidated. Moreover, standardized treatments for this transformation are lacking. We present a case of lung adenocarcinoma with the 19del mutation transforming into SCLC post osimertinib treatment. By integrating this case with existing literature, we aim to share insights into diagnosing and treating small cell transformation, hoping to draw attention to this issue.
Case presentation
In May 2020, a 44-year-old female nonsmoker with lung adenocarcinoma presented to our hospital complaining of chest tightness and shortness of breath. The patient underwent a curative operation in January 2019. The pathological findings were as follows: moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma (stage IB, pT2 Visc PI N0M0) with an EGFR exon 19del mutation. An adjuvant chemotherapy regimen of nedaplatin (75 mg/m² on day 1) combined with pemetrexed (500 mg/m² on day 1) was conducted for four cycles after the surgery. The chemotherapy course was uneventful, showing no progression of lung cancer markers or computed tomography findings (Fig. 1) (Fig. 2a and b). Clinical features and treatment details are summarized in Tables 1 and 2, respectively.

Head MRI revealed an abnormal subcortical signal in the right parietal lobe. Chest-enhanced computed tomography demonstrated enlarged small nodules in the right lung’s upper lobe, multiple nodules in both lungs, and pleural masses (Fig. 1). Given the EGFR 19del mutation identified in a previous genetic test, the patient was advised to initiate targeted therapy with osimertinib (80 mg/day). Following treatment with osimertinib, the patient’s cerebral lesions and scattered pulmonary nodules resolved, yet the pleural mass persisted. Abdominal computed tomography in January 2022 revealed right adrenal metastasis (Fig. 1), with the disease progressing to a progression-free survival (PFS) of 7.8 months. A puncture biopsy of the left pleural mass in January 2022 and subsequent HE staining identified diffuse, small round tumor cells without glandular ductal formation, exhibiting obvious heterogeneity, leading to a diagnosis of SCLC (Fig. 2c and d). Immunohistochemical results were as follows: CD56 (+), Syn (+), PCK (+), Napsin A (+), CgA (+), TTF-1 (+), INSM1 (+), CK8/18 (+), P63 (−), P40 (−), and Ki67(+, 80%). The patient underwent lung radiotherapy (30 Gy/5 fractions) and combination chemotherapy with etoposide (160 mg/day) and cisplatin (40 mg/day), resulting in disease stabilization.
In September 2022, a biopsy of a newly identified thyroid nodule was conducted, revealing neuroendocrine carcinoma of the thyroid gland (small cell type) (Fig. 2e and f), suggestive of pulmonary origin. The patient received one cycle of irinotecan (100 mg/day) chemotherapy, followed by five cycles of combination therapy with irinotecan (100 mg/day) and atezolizumab (1.2 g/day), which failed to achieve significant remission. Hepatic metastases developed during treatment (Fig. 1). Concurrently, owing to ongoing enlargement of the thyroid and adrenal glands, thyroid radiotherapy (50 Gy/25 fractions) and adrenal radiotherapy (40 Gy/20 fraction) were administered on 1 February 2023. Upon developing multiple brain metastases, the patient underwent cranial radiotherapy (30 Gy/10 fractions, only completed 2 fractions). The patient succumbed to the disease on 11 May 2023, with an overall survival (OS) of 52.7 months, attributable to disease progression and organ failure.
Literature review
Transformation mechanisms: lung adenocarcinoma to small cell lung cancer
The mechanisms driving the conversion of nonsmall cell lung cancer (NSCLC) to SCLC after EGFR-TKI therapy remain ambiguous. Three predominant theories may explain this phenomenon: (1) The tumor cell heterogeneity hypothesis posits that SCLC and lung adenocarcinoma coexist at the tumor’s initial stage. During EGFR-TKI treatment, adenocarcinoma cells are suppressed and subsequently replaced by proliferating SCLC cells, which form SCLC histological subtypes. The limited number of pathological specimens from core biopsies or fine-needle aspirations precludes comprehensive molecular testing to determine the coexistence of lung adenocarcinoma and SCLC. Mixed lung cancers typically represent 1–3.2% of all SCLC cases, but postsurgical pathology reveals a higher incidence, between 9 and 26%, of mixed lung cancers [3]. This indicates that the volume of specimens significantly affects the detection of SCLC. Should tumor heterogeneity be the cause, the cancer would likely not have responded as effectively to osimertinib and would have developed resistance more rapidly. (2) The tumor stem cell hypothesis posits that tumor stem cells harboring sensitive mutations possess the potential to differentiate into neuroendocrine tumor cells. Treatment with EGFR-TKIs resulted in the preservation of resistant lung adenocarcinoma cells, which subsequently transformed into SCLC. Despite being distinct histological subtypes, SCLC and NSCLC may have a common cellular origin, as evidence suggests [4]. A retrospective study found that the types of EGFR mutations identified before and after transformation were broadly consistent, strongly suggesting that transformed SCLC is not de novo but derives from NSCLC [5]. (3) The molecular mechanism hypothesis: dual deletions in TP53 and RB1 are pivotal in the transformation to SCLC during TKI treatment. Lee et al. [6] discovered that the inactivation of TP53 and RB1 at initial diagnosis amplifies the relative risk of histologic transformation in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma by 42.8 times. A multicenter retrospective study in China, however, revealed that 28% of patients lacked mutations in either TP53 or RB1 at the time of transformation [7], indicating that mutations in TP53 and RB1 are not definitive predictors of SCLC transformation. Some lung adenocarcinomas harboring TP53 and RB1 mutations did not transition to SCLC, underscoring the necessity of additional factors for histologic transformation [8]. While myelocytomatosis oncogene amplification is absent in primary tumors, it emerges in transformed SCLC and may be associated with histological transformation [9]. Research has demonstrated that genome-wide enrichment of whole-genome doubling and apolipoprotein-B mRNA-editing complex signaling occurs in EGFR/TP53/RB1 mutant lung adenocarcinomas undergoing small cell transformation, implying a contributory role in this process [4]. Small cell transformation seldom occurs in KRAS mutant lung adenocarcinomas [10]. Besides the factors above, SCLC transformation could also be linked to TERT amplification [11], PIK3CA mutations [12], and epithelial-mesenchymal transition [13,14].
Treatment strategies for transformed small cell lung cancer
Compared to lung adenocarcinoma, transformed SCLC more closely resembles classical SCLC regarding mRNA expression profiles, genetic characteristics, and clinical manifestations [15]. Consequently, the treatment regimen for transformed SCLC may closely parallel that of primary SCLC. Once lung adenocarcinoma transforms into SCLC, it progresses rapidly, leading to a poor prognosis with a median survival of 10.9 months posttransformation [16]. EGFR protein expression significantly decreases posttransformation, diminishing the tumor’s responsiveness to EGFR-TKIs [15]. Combination chemotherapy with EGFR-TKIs, however, can delay drug resistance and the timing of transformation in patients with EGFR/TP53/RB1 triple mutations and is recommended for transformed SCLC. The efficacy and safety of this combination will be evaluated in a clinical trial (NCT03567642) [8]. Wang et al. [17] concluded that first-line treatment combining chemotherapy and EGFR-TKIs after SCLC transformation extended PFS compared to chemotherapy alone, yet offered no OS advantage. No standard treatment exists for transformed SCLC, and platinum-based dual-agent therapy continues to be employed, drawing on the treatment strategy for primary SCLC [18]. A retrospective study involving 58 individuals reported a median transformation time of 17.8 months. After transformation, clinical responses were observed in 54% of the 46 patients receiving etoposide and platinum and 50% of the 20 patients treated with paclitaxel. None of the 17 patients treated with immunotherapy, however, responded. The study revealed that most transformed SCLCs are chemosensitive, particularly showing better responses to initial etoposide and cisplatin chemotherapy. Etoposide and cisplatin chemotherapy have been clinically proven to be viable and effective treatments for small cell transformations following EGFR-TKIs treatment failure [16]. Both PFS and OS, however, are shorter following first-line conventional chemotherapy. Compared to conventional chemotherapy, combination therapy (incorporating chemotherapy with radiotherapy, targeted therapy, or both) yielded a longer median PFS (4 months vs. 7 months), albeit without a significant difference in median OS (8 months vs. 9 months) [19]. Antiangiogenic therapy and local radiotherapy have been shown to extend OS following transformation significantly [17]. Despite the controversy surrounding antiangiogenic therapies in primary SCLC treatment [20–22], anlotinib emerges as a viable option for patients with transformed SCLC, achieving an objective response rate of 66.7% and median PFS of 6.2 months in those treated with anlotinib [7]. Patients treated with anlotinib experienced longer OS than those not receiving antivascular agents [17]. Antivascular drugs may offer potential benefits in small cell transformation; however, further research is required to determine the optimal timing for drug administration and selection. Radiation therapy may significantly extend OS posttransformation compared with patients who do not undergo such treatment [17]. This sensitivity may be attributable to the inherent characteristics of SCLC, which is notably responsive to radiation therapy [17]. The retention of the original EGFR mutation in subsequent biopsies posthistological transformation indicates that these tumors maintain NSCLC mutational characteristics, hence exhibiting poor responsiveness to immune checkpoint inhibitors [23]. In multiple studies, patients with transformed SCLC exhibited no response to immunotherapy (nivolumab) [16,24]. ABT-263, a developed inhibitor of the BCL-2 family proteins, interrupts the interaction between BCL-2 and Bim by binding to BCL-2 [25], inducing apoptosis in SCLC transformed from EGFR-mutant adenocarcinoma [15]. Previous research indicated that combining zeste homolog 2 inhibitors with EGFR-TKIs can prevent histologic transformation in NSCLC with triple mutations in EGFR/TP53/RB1 [14]. Various drugs targeting the RB1 mutation in transformed SCLC, including checkpoint kinase 1, polo-like kinase 1, and aurora kinase a (AURKA) inhibitors, show promise in treating transformed SCLC. An ongoing phase 1/1b clinical trial is currently enrolling patients to compare the efficacy of the AURKA inhibitor alisertib with osimertinib in treating metastatic EGFR-mutant cancers (NCT04085315) [26].
Discussion
Regular biopsies in lung cancer patients undergoing EGFR-TKI treatment enable the detection of EGFR mutations and histological transformations [27], facilitating timely adjustments to the treatment regimen based on varying resistance mechanisms [28]. When tissue biopsy is not feasible, liquid biopsy offers a practical alternative [29]. Liquid biopsy enables tracking resistance mechanism changes during tumor progression in TKI-treated patients by monitoring blood samples for tumor-derived components, including circulating tumor cells and circulating tumor DNA [30]. Additionally, liquid biopsies can monitor biomarkers in advanced lung adenocarcinoma [31].
SCLC is more aggressive than lung adenocarcinoma and necessitates timely identification of pathological transformation at an early stage. The inactivation of TP53 and RB1 is a reliable predictor for SCLC transformation during EGFR-TKI treatment of lung adenocarcinoma [6,32]. In the absence of TP53 and RB1 detection during EGFR-TKI treatment, additional indicators or clinical features, however, are essential for early recognition [17]. Following the completion of four cycles of pemetrexed–nedaplatin combination chemotherapy in April 2019, the patient did not undergo re-evaluation until May 2020. Unfortunately, by this time, the cancer had progressed to stage IV, highlighting the necessity for regular and timely follow-up appointments for lung cancer patients. After disease progression post osimertinib therapy, lung biopsies confirmed the transformation into SCLC. In this case, the patient’s pro-gastrin releasing peptide (ProGRP) and neuron-specific enolase (NSE) levels were first abnormally elevated in October 2021, reaching 300.00 pg/ml (normal value ≤65.70) (Fig. 3) and 40.84 µg/l (normal value <16.30) (Fig. 4), respectively, indicating potential small cell transformation. Since February 2022, the serum NSE levels have consistently exceeded the normal range, further suggesting histologic transformation. Nevertheless, a lung biopsy conducted in January 2022 confirmed the pathological diagnosis of SCLC. The detection of tumor markers indicative of small cell transformation preceded the findings from pathological biopsies. Figures 3 and 4 demonstrate that ProGRP and NSE may predict small cell transformation; however, these predictions’ correlation strength require further validation in subsequent studies. Currently, effective standard treatment modalities are lacking, necessitating an enhanced understanding of translational mechanisms and the identification of new targets to improve outcomes. While understanding the field’s current state through existing studies is beneficial, the predominance of case reports and small retrospective studies, coupled with a scarcity of prospective and extensive retrospective studies, remains a challenge. Unfortunately, this case report lacks extensive molecular testing. Moving forward, we aim to explore the clinical and molecular characteristics, as well as the prognosis of patients who have experienced transformation to SCLC, using either prospective or large-scale retrospective studies, with the ultimate goal of identifying more effective treatment strategies following transformation.
Conclusions
In patients with EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinomas resistant to EGFR-TKIs, rapid disease progression and significant elevations in ProGRP and NSE levels indicate the need for evaluating potential pathological transformation. Repeat biopsies are necessary even after the initial pathological diagnosis following surgery, emphasizing the importance of ongoing monitoring. Additionally, we suggest assessing TP53 and RB1 status in patients receiving EGFR-TKI therapy, along with continuous mutation testing, to enable prompt adjustments in treatment regimens.
